claims.text: The starting powder blend is equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi.
Ten hours of high-energy ball milling will induce severe plastic deformation, amorphization, supersaturation, and a high defect density.
SPS at 950°C, 100°C/min, a five-minute dwell, and 50 MPa is an effective rapid-consolidation regime for equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi.
A displacement rate corresponding to an approximately constant densification strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 should be maintained.
A vacuum below 10^-3 Pa will prevent oxidation during SPS.
The milling-plus-SPS treatment will suppress porosity and produce greater than 99.5% density.
The processed alloy will have an average grain size of 20–50 nm.
The resulting phase constitution will be a dominant FCC matrix containing 5–10% BCC precipitates.
Rapid SPS will suppress brittle, Ti-rich HCP phase formation that would occur during slow cooling or prolonged thermal equilibration.
Milling-induced dislocations and grain boundaries lower the activation energy for nucleation of the FCC solid solution.
Milling-induced defects raise the barrier to diffusion-controlled separation of Ti-rich HCP phases.
A high heating rate and short SPS dwell limit grain growth and solute segregation.
The applied pressure closes pores before significant grain coarsening occurs.
The nanocrystalline FCC/BCC alloy will exhibit a Vickers hardness of 450–550 HV, with grain refinement being a principal source of the increase.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi has 2–5% porosity, a coarse single-phase FCC structure, and a hardness of 150–200 HV.
Sintering above 1050°C will promote HCP formation and grain growth.
Milling for less than ten hours will not produce the supersaturation and defect density required by the proposed mechanism.
Titanium addition generally increases hardness, strength, and wear resistance because of its relatively large atomic radius.
Local heating at extreme milling strain rates could trigger premature HCP nucleation.
If a nanocrystalline sample is softer than a coarse-grained sample having the same phase composition, the Hall–Petch grain-refinement mechanism is falsified.

contradictions.description: The SPS temperature is described as both 'just below the solidus' and approximately 0.6 Tm. A temperature near 0.6 Tm is ordinarily well below the solidus, so these descriptions do not define a consistent thermal position without a system-specific solidus value.

The design specifies nanoindentation at 10 mN for 10 seconds, whereas the listed hardness measurement is Vickers hardness. No Vickers indentation load or dwell time is supplied, and nanoindentation hardness is not directly identical to an HV value.

The falsification rule invokes a coarse-grained and nanocrystalline pair with the same phase composition, but the actual slow-sintered control deliberately changes phase stability and the reduced-milling control changes alloying and defect state. The required phase-matched grain-size control is therefore not present in the design.
